q: A fraud model validated well, but three months after deployment precision falls while the confirmed-fraud rate is unchanged and several input feature distributions have visibly moved. The best diagnosis is:
a: covariate shift: the input distribution has moved away from the training one
b: concept drift: the same inputs now correspond to a different fraud outcome
c: label leakage: a feature encodes the very outcome it is meant to predict
d: overfitting: the model memorised noise present in the training split
explain: Movement in the inputs with a stable outcome rate is covariate (data) drift. Concept drift tempts because performance also decays, but it is a change in the input-to-outcome mapping and would not announce itself through shifted input distributions; leakage and overfitting would already show at validation.

q: A credit-scoring model's input distributions are stable month over month, yet defaults among approved applicants climb steadily after an interest-rate shock. This pattern indicates:
a: covariate shift: the applicant population has moved since training
b: training-serving skew: serving transforms differ from the training ones
c: concept drift: the mapping from features to outcome has itself changed
d: sampling bias: the training set under-represented rejected applicants
explain: Stable inputs with a degrading outcome relationship is concept drift — P(y|X) moved while P(X) did not. Covariate shift is the tempting mirror image, but it requires the inputs themselves to move, which the monitoring explicitly rules out.

q: A churn model evaluates well offline but online precision is far lower; the serving path turns out to compute 'days since last login' in a different timezone from the training job. The systemic fix is:
a: raise retraining frequency so the model absorbs the serving-time values
b: add the timezone as an input feature so the model can correct for it
c: monitor the offline and online feature distributions and alert on divergence
d: compute the feature once from a shared definition used by training and serving
explain: This is training-serving skew: one definition served to both paths — the point of a feature store — removes the class of bug rather than the instance. Monitoring is the tempting answer because it would have caught this one, but detection after the fact still leaves every future feature free to diverge.

q: A team ports its established software CI/CD to an ML service. Which addition most distinguishes an ML delivery pipeline from a software one?
a: versioned data and model artefacts with validation gates before promotion
b: container images pinned by digest and promoted unchanged across environments
c: unit and integration tests executed on every commit before the build is published
d: blue-green infrastructure so that a failed release can be reverted within seconds
explain: ML adds artefacts (data, models) and a statistical acceptance criterion that code tests cannot express. The other three are good practice but are ordinary software CI/CD, present with or without a model.

q: Before changing both the prompt and the base model of a live assistant, a team wants a cheap, repeatable signal for behaviour regressions. The standard instrument is:
a: a fresh sample of recent production traffic, scored by a judge model after each release
b: a golden set (golden dataset) of fixed inputs with known-good reference outputs
c: a held-out slice of the fine-tuning data, rescored after every prompt revision
d: weekly aggregated user thumb ratings, compared across the two prompt versions
explain: A fixed input set with reference outputs is what makes two releases comparable at all — the regression suite of an LLM system. Scoring fresh production traffic is tempting and useful for coverage, but with the inputs changing every run it cannot separate a behaviour regression from a change in the traffic.

q: A team ranks answer quality by having an LLM judge compare pairs of candidate answers. Which safeguard most directly addresses the judge's documented biases?
a: a judge from a different vendor than the model under test, run at temperature zero
b: averaging three independent judge runs and reporting the median score per item
c: asking the judge to state its reasoning before it emits the final numeric score
d: an explicit rubric with randomised option order, calibrated against human ratings
explain: Position bias is addressed by randomising order, verbosity and vagueness by an explicit rubric, and overall validity by periodic human calibration. A different-vendor judge is the tempting answer but only addresses self-preference, leaving position and verbosity bias untouched.

q: A ministry is about to release a public-facing assistant. Which activity qualifies as red-teaming rather than ordinary testing?
a: adversarial probing for harmful, policy-violating or data-leaking behaviour
b: load testing the endpoint at three times the expected peak concurrency for an hour
c: scoring the golden set after each prompt change and gating the release
d: reviewing a sample of production conversations for answer accuracy
explain: Red-teaming is adversarial by design: someone actively tries to make the system misbehave, including jailbreaks, misuse framings and injection. Golden-set scoring is the tempting near-miss, but it measures expected behaviour on known inputs rather than searching for unknown failure modes.

q: An assistant must answer from a document corpus that is amended weekly, and each answer must cite its source. The architecture that satisfies both requirements is:
a: fine-tuning weekly on the amended corpus, with the source recorded in the answer
b: a long system prompt containing the corpus, refreshed whenever a document changes
c: retrieval at query time over a versioned store, with retrieved passages cited
d: a cached question-and-answer store, rebuilt from the corpus after each amendment
explain: Retrieval separates volatile knowledge from the model and makes the cited passage an actual object the answer was conditioned on. Weekly fine-tuning is the tempting alternative, but it gives no traceable source for any individual claim and turns every amendment into a training run.

q: Users report an assistant answering 'not found in the documents' for questions whose answer has sat in the indexed corpus for months; pasting the passage in manually produces a correct answer. The fault lies in:
a: retrieval — chunking or embedding mismatch keeps the passage out of the context
b: generation — the model declines to answer despite having the evidence available
c: prompting — the instructions never tell the model to use the retrieved context
d: freshness — the newest documents have not yet been added to the search index
explain: The manual-paste test isolates the stages: given the evidence, generation succeeds, so the failure is upstream. Index freshness is the plausible rival but the stem places the answer in the corpus already, leaving chunk granularity, embedding fit or filtering as the cause.

q: A retrieval system over long legal acts returns precise snippets that lack the surrounding definitions needed to answer correctly. The most targeted change is:
a: raise top-k so that more of the small chunks enter the context per question
b: retrieve small chunks, then expand each hit to its parent section
c: increase chunk size uniformly so every chunk carries more surrounding text
d: lower the similarity threshold so neighbouring borderline chunks are admitted
explain: Parent-document expansion keeps retrieval precise while restoring the context the answer needs. Uniformly larger chunks is the tempting blunt version: it dilutes embedding relevance for every query and spends context on text nobody asked about.
